articles.title: Women targeted by police officers who 'abused the badge'
articles.summary: Two women preyed upon by serving police officers describe their ordeals and why they are speaking out.
articles.body:
Two women who were preyed upon by serving police officers they trusted have described their ordeals and why they decided to speak out.

Naomi Meadows was raped by a detective she met online in Devon, while Catherine Dobson was subjected to years of coercive and controlling behaviour by a Lancashire police officer who worked in a sexual offences unit.

Catherine said: "He used his job, he used his power and he abused the badge. Whatever his motives were, I will never understand."

The women waived their right to anonymity to tell their harrowing stories as part of a BBC investigation that uncovered more than 1,200 domestic abuse allegations made in three years against police officers and special constables across England and Wales.

Professional standards investigations were opened into allegations including rape, sexual assault, grievous bodily harm, stalking and serious violence.

Most cases were discontinued, subjected to no further action or dropped because of a lack of evidence or victims withdrawing their complaints.

Campaigners say more needs to be done to tackle police-perpetrated abuse despite repeated warnings about failures to identify and remove dangerous officers in the wake of the 2021 murder of Sarah Everard in London by serving Metropolitan Police officer Wayne Couzens.

Catherine Dobson, from Rawtenstall in Lancashire, said she was asked out for a drink by Michael Harvey after a chance meeting in a supermarket.

"The only reason I trusted him was because he told me he was a detective in the police," she said.

"We got on really well: this was a man who was paid to look after the most vulnerable in society - women and children who'd been abused - so that made me feel safe."

What Catherine did not realise was that Harvey had already accessed police computer systems to obtain her address and phone number.

Cracks appeared early on in their relationship.

Catherine grew suspicious that Harvey had not introduced her to his children and would not let her post pictures of them together online.

When she discovered Harvey had been texting other women, she was told they were victims of sexual offences he was investigating.

Catherine said she had no reason to disbelieve him.

"At the time I backed off because who am I to stop a victim of a crime like that from being supported by the officer?"

It was when she tried to end the relationship that the psychological abuse escalated.

Catherine said he told her he had been abused as a child and later made unfounded claims he had been tested for cancer.

"I believed him," she said. "I felt responsible for keeping him well."

Catherine believes it was part of a pattern of emotional manipulation designed to stop her leaving.

She said Harvey threatened to take his own life on several occasions if she left him, including once during a phone call while she was at work.

"I called the police immediately, then I drove back to the house and I was in bits," she said. "I honestly thought I'd open the door and find him dead.

"The police were there and they were just about to bash the door in when he calmly opened it wrapped in a towel and he said, 'What's the problem officer? I've just been in the shower'.

"I felt like this hysterical mess who'd made the whole thing up. But when you're in it, you're not thinking straight."

During years of emotional blackmail, Catherine described how Harvey had faked an anaphylactic shock and threatened to jump out of a moving car.

She eventually left him, but it was another six years before she filed a police report.

Explaining her hesitation, she said: "Who is going to believe me over a detective on the sex offenders' unit?"

Harvey was arrested in 2023 and was jailed earlier this year. He was sentenced to two-and-a-half years after admitting coercive and controlling behaviour and the unauthorised use of police computers. He was cleared of three counts of rape.

Lancashire Constabulary described Harvey's behaviour as "abhorrent" and said it had "no place in policing".

The force said it remained committed to protecting women and girls.

The BBC understands another woman complained to the force about Harvey before he met Catherine but was told he had not committed an offence.

Lancashire Constabulary declined to comment, citing an ongoing complaints process.

Harvey's case was not an isolated incident.

The BBC sent Freedom of Information requests to 45 police forces across England and Wales, asking for details of domestic abuse allegations involving police officers.

Just over half responded, disclosing a total of 1,280 cases investigated by professional standards departments in the three years to January.

The allegations included rape, sexual assault, coercive control, stalking and non-fatal strangulation.

Former Merseyside PC Ryan Theaker was jailed earlier this month for 11 years .

A court heard his victim had told him to "get off me" more than 300 times as he subjected her to an 82-minute ordeal in a Liverpool hotel room.

Theaker was one of few convicted of a criminal offence, however.

Most concluded cases resulted in no further action, including 96% in the North West.

Nearly half of the 1,280 cases in England and Wales disclosed to the BBC were recorded by the largest force, the Metropolitan Police.

Dozens of its officers were accused of rape or other sexual offences.

Devon and Cornwall PC Stuart Mines was convicted last year of rape.

He met Naomi Meadows on a dating website before they agreed to meet in person.

Naomi told the BBC: "You kind of have a childlike trust because they're the police - they're honest, trustworthy."

After a dog walk together, Mines invited her back to his home for Sunday lunch.

Naomi said she quickly felt uncomfortable.

She said Mines had smacked her backside and repeatedly talked about being a police officer and the authority that came with the role.

"I felt intimidated," said Naomi. "I felt scared. Then things just went from bad to worse - he raped me."

Naomi, from Exeter, said she had been too frightened to leave.

"Physically he was bigger than me and he obviously had all this power because he was a police officer.

"His uniform was hanging up and he had all his badges on. You just do what you can to survive, I guess."

For months afterwards, Naomi remained silent.

"I didn't trust the police to investigate it because he was one of their own," she said.

When she did speak out, Mines was arrested and charged. He was later convicted of rape and jailed for eight years.

Naomi said her battle had not ended with his conviction.

A subsequent professional standards department investigation upheld a number of complaints about the way in which Devon and Cornwall Police had handled her case and concluded it was "not acceptable".

The investigation found she should have been told Mines had been suspended.

The BBC has also learned he continued to be paid for a month after his conviction.

Naomi said the failings had left her feeling abandoned.

"I wasn't told that he was suspended," she said. "So I stayed in my house for months because I was worried he'd be walking the streets."

She added she had not received victim care support from police because the file was restricted.

Devon and Cornwall Police acknowledged failings identified following Naomi's complaint, including that Mines continued to receive police pay after his conviction when he should not have done.

The force said lessons had been learned, procedures changed and additional safeguards introduced for victims of police-perpetrated abuse.

Campaigners said the figures for England and Wales reflected a wider problem that police forces had struggled to confront.

Former police officer Bridie Anderson, who now supports victims of police-perpetrated abuse, says officers can use the trust and authority that comes with their badge to exert power over victims.

"What we know about domestic abusers is that they present a front to the rest of the world that is very different to the one the survivor sees," she said.

Anderson said cases involving police officers presented unique challenges because perpetrators often had immediate credibility with colleagues and the public, while victims may fear they would not be believed.

The Women Against Rape campaign group said the BBC's investigation raised serious questions about whether policing had learned the lessons of the Everard case and subsequent reviews.

It said victims of police abuse often faced an additional hurdle because they had to report their allegations to the force employing the alleged perpetrator.

Chief Constable Chris Todd, the National Police Chiefs' Council's lead for professional standards, said police recognised the "devastating impact" of these crimes and the fear victims may feel about reporting an abuser who was part of the organisation meant to protect them.

He said forces had strengthened vetting and misconduct procedures, increased dismissals for gross misconduct and were determined to identify and remove officers who should not be in policing.

Naomi said her decision to waive her anonymity had not been about herself, but about "what needs to change".

"So many men get away with abusing women and girls and don't face any consequences and when it's police-perpetrated crime, they should be held to a higher account," she said.

"The people with the means to change these things need to listen to what we've had to go through and the little support we've had."

For Catherine, the effects of Harvey's abuse remain years later.

"It changed me as a person," she said. "I've never been the same since."

Of the man who abused her, she added: "He knew what he were doing. I couldn't keep him out of my house, I couldn't keep him out of my head. And I had no say."

articles.title: Bath residents say Curo has 'failed' them over service charges
articles.summary: Housing association Curo defends large increases to leaseholder bills.
articles.body:
A housing association has defended the charges faced by its leaseholders after many complained of huge bill increases to pay for maintenance.

Callum Maddern, who lives in Bath, said he had seen his service charge increase six-fold to more than £8,000 per year after Curo said vital work needed doing on his accommodation block.

"I didn't have enough money to put the heating on," he said. "I had water on my sink and coffee tables that was freezing. I'd be lying in bed and I could see my breath."

Curo, which says it does not make any money from the contributions, said it was "trying to work with residents to prepare them for these bills".

Man jailed for 'cruel' attack that killed pensioner

Community ownership could restore city landmark

Student who murdered uni housemate jailed for life

When Maddern bought his flat in 2023, the annual service charge was about £1,300 per year. He was told there was £5,000 in what is known as a sinking fund to cover any necessary works.

But the following year, he received a bill for £8,000 to go towards fire safety work and new windows.

"Originally I thought there was some kind of mistake," he said. But when he queried the charge, Curo confirmed it was accurate.

Maddern describes "constant delays" in his attempts to reach out to Curo and negotiate.

"They were totally uncaring," he said, adding he was told he could sell his property and pay the fee that way.

Maddern said he ended up selling possessions and taking out loans to pay for the work.

While he said he knew that as a leaseholder he had a responsibility to contribute towards maintenance costs, he questioned why everything suddenly had to be done in a three-year period.

"If new windows are needed, absolutely that must be scheduled in. But to have everything in the space of three years, surely that is not a good approach," he added.

Andrew Snee, director of housing and support at Curo, acknowledged the way charges had been communicated could have been better and said he wanted to apologise "if our correspondence has caused any concern or upset".

But Snee denied the company could have managed the costs better, describing the situation as a "perfect storm".

"The cost of living is increasing, the cost of contracts is increasing, at the same time we've got increased legislation around property safety and fire safety, which has to be a good thing but it does come at a cost," he said.

"We are being as honest and transparent as we can to deliver these costs in as caring a way as we can. Keep talking to us."

Ken Pearson owns his flat in a different block elsewhere in Bath.

He says his sinking fund contributions dropped to £124 per year when Curo took over his building, but then increased dramatically to £1,767 when a new roof was needed.

"We were only being prepared for the new roof when it was a matter of urgency because two flats upstairs had leaks," he said. "We should have paid over a longer period."

Pearson took Curo to a tribunal over the sinking fund increases and lost his case, but now believes there needs to be a change in the law to ensure that landlords prepare leaseholders better for expected works.

"Curo have failed us and need to be held to account," he said. "They have not picked up that there was this financial catastrophe coming along."

In response, Snee said: "I think sinking funds have been managed as well as we can in today's world with all of the pressures on costs and contracts."

He added: "If you've been building a sinking fund up and decoration has taken place, that would have potentially drawn quite a lot out.

"Then if you're looking at a roof replacement in four to five years' time, not only are you looking at paying for that you're also starting from zero."

The government is working on a new law that would ban the use of leasehold for most new flats and create a new right for leaseholders to request improvements.

articles.title: Girl with muscular dystrophy gets own Bristol Fashion billboard
articles.summary: Carmela, who has muscular dystrophy, says it was "amazing" to see herself on the billboard.
articles.body:
A 12-year-old girl has been surprised with her own billboard after campaigning for greater disability representation in fashion.

Carmela Chillery-Watson MBE, from Wiltshire, lives with LMNA congenital muscular dystrophy - a progressive muscle-wasting condition.

On Wednesday, she was given a surprise at the Arches on Cheltenham Road in Bristol, when she turned a corner with her family and saw herself on a billboard for the very first time.

It was organised by the Bristol Fashion Show, a volunteer-run collective of designers and artists from across the South West who work to create a platform "for those too often overlooked by the fashion industry".

Healthcare workers walk out on 24-hour strike

Gender critical teacher 'could have shown respect'

M4 to be closed overnight for landslide repairs

"I had no clue what was going to happen, it was a bit of a mystery coming here," said Carmela.

"I never been on a billboard before, so that's amazing."

Currently living in Dorset, Carmela said it was important for people "with all abilities to be able to do fashion" and she hoped to see catwalk shows include more people from disabled backgrounds.

The 12-year-old continued: "Wheelchairs, walkers, walking sticks... I really hope in the future it will become more normalised."

Carmela has been part of the Bristol Fashion Show since she was five and taken part in various catwalks.

Carmela has raised thousands of pounds for both Muscular Dystrophy UK and Julia's House Hospice in the past and has often completed her fundraisers while dressed in superhero costumes.

In December, she became the youngest person ever to receive an MBE when she met Prince William at Windsor Castle.

Mum Lucy said there were "no words" to express her pride for her daughter and the new billboard.

"I'm so excited and proud of her," she said.

"Growing up, Carmela loved to dress up and we signed her up with some modelling agencies aged five but she just wasn't getting any jobs after a few years.

"She turned round and asked me 'am I ugly? Do they not want me to model for them?' So I took it upon myself... and found the Bristol Fashion Show."

Organisers of the Bristol Fashion Show said they wanted to continue to increase the inclusivity with their event, considering factors like age, disability and background.

Butzi Schlaadt, who founded the show in 2012, still remembers when Carmela first got involved.

She recalled: "Her mum rang me six or seven years ago and said it was her [Carmela's] dream to model, and I said, 'of course she can model'. She's been with us ever since, she's incredible."

This year's Bristol Fashion Show will take place on 1 November. The show raises money for Cure4Carmela, her family's fundraising initiative which supports Muscular Dystrophy UK.

Co-organiser Charly Evans said she had spoken to Carmela about her hopes for this year's show - and found out many people with disabilities, hidden and visible, did not feel represented.

"We felt it was our mission to change that," she said.

"We have given all our designers the challenge this year to design an outfit for someone with a disability, visible or invisible, and they are working with the models directly."

articles.title: Wolverhampton mother and daughter duo make funny videos to tackle grief
articles.summary: A mother and daughter have turned their grief into a huge online following with uplifting videos.
articles.body:
A Wolverhampton mother and her 11-year-old daughter have become internet sensations after amassing millions of views across Instagram and TikTok with videos of their morning routines, dances and song parodies.

"We turned [our] pain into purpose because, behind everything, there's been a lot of struggle," said Amn, who together with daughter, Ria, have been making social media videos to bring a smile to their community.

The duo started making content as a way of helping their family cope with the sudden death of Amn's father in 2023, and also to provide a platform to help break down stigmas within the South Asian community.

"It [also] comes from a place of a lot of pain, being a young mum, giving birth to a daughter when the expectations around you were those of a son," Amn told BBC Radio WM.

Amn added: "I was 22 when I had Ria and, all these years on, I've taught her, 'Girl, no matter what knocks you down, we just get back up and we get better and better and better.'

"You get overwhelmed because there's so much pressure for you to do so well, especially in the South Asian community. The pressure is intense."

Former tennis club site serves up new council homes

Care home rated inadequate again amid safety fears

'Alice Cooper is a character, like Jekyll and Hyde'

The Wolverhampton mother spoke candidly of her struggles after losing her father, and the impact this had on her relationship with her daughter and husband, Jag.

Looking back, she added: "There was a time when I went through a little bit of a blip, where I felt I wasn't being the best mum.

"I did my best for her, but she was small at the time and she'd see me get knocked down and she'd be like my sister and she'd pick me up. She'd be like, 'Mum, it's okay, we'll be all right'.

"When dad passed away, I wasn't the best mother or wife to these two, and my mum, sisters and brothers saw it happening.

"Jag picked everything up and Ria was like, 'Mum, it's okay. I've got you'.

Both parents are musicians. Amn is a singer and Jag plays the tabla drums, so they draw on their backgrounds to help create uplifting videos.

Their first clip to go viral amassed more than one million views and showed them reworking Disney's Frozen hit, Do You Want to Build a Snowman? with new lyrics to become Do You Want to Build Your Son's Wife?

Amn said: "We started receiving messages from people saying, 'You're helping me', and 'You're showing me how to be a better mum to my daughter', because initially it is about showing her the sky is the limit.

"We make songs and I make songs with lyrics that people can sing to their kids and their grandkids, because through music you can love.

"I think the biggest thing through social media is the connections. I've made friendships. I've made friends who have moved from London to the West Midlands. I've missed having that circle, but I'm now meeting so many lovely people.

"You're coming across so many like-minded people who are helping us build connections, and it's taking us places."

articles.title: Why do farmers want to build reservoirs and what's stopping them?
articles.summary: Farmers are calling for less red tape and more government funding to help them build reservoirs on their land.
articles.body:
In the face of climate change, farmers are calling for less red tape and more government funding to help them build reservoirs on their land.

They say storing more water on farmland could help reduce flooding in the winter, minimise the impact of drought in the summer and provide food security.

The reservoirs would hold winter rainwater to be used on their crops in summer.

The government is poised to launch a £15m scheme to go towards up to 100 farm reservoirs, but some farmers say that is a "drop in the ocean".

Man jailed for 'cruel' attack that killed pensioner

Glastonbury coach tickets oversold in admin error

Healthcare workers walk out on 24-hour strike

Arable farmers with crops like potatoes, high-value salad, apples and pears are among those calling for solutions to their water shortages.

Philip Vaux's potatoes are destined to become posh crisps.

He farms at South Petherton in Somerset with his son and remembers the summer of 1976 but said this year has been "much drier - exceptionally dry".

"All crops have been affected, we're getting poor yields in the cereals and potatoes - for the livestock industry it's hard graft to find enough fodder for animals," he said.

They rent 30 acres which has a borehole and has been able to be irrigated, but on the rest of their 300-acre farm, yields are down around two-thirds.

Vaux said they are seeing the effects of climate change, first-hand.

"We've had two dry summers now, this year and last year. The previous two summers were very wet. So we've gone from one extreme to another."

He has changed the type of potatoes they are planting to try and find drought-resistant varieties.

A few miles away in south Somerset, James Pullen said this year's harvest of potatoes and cider apples would have been a "total disaster" if it was not for his two on-farm reservoirs.

Holding five million gallons (22 million litres) between them, he said they are now "totally empty".

Even with the water, he said his potatoes were smaller this year.

"If we are going to have a continuation of these hot dry summers it's essential we have more water storage," Pullen said.

"Anyone who's seriously growing root crops would definitely need to be able to water them because they do need an excessive amount of water, but then it's not easy for some people because you do need a reasonable block of land."

As well as needing space to build a reservoir, and potentially a source of water like a stream to top-up the winter rainfall, the cost of building a reservoir can be prohibitive for farmers.

Philip Vaux said it can be "exceptionally expensive" with a reservoir "costing thousands and taking ten years to get your money back" in improved crop yields.

"It's no good just digging a hole and hoping the water is going to stay there," said Vaux.

As a smaller-scale alternative he put in a second borehole last year at a cost of around £12,000 but they need to find another £8-10,000 to connect it to a pumping system to get the water out to the fields.

The Country Land and Business Association (CLA) is a membership organisation for owners of land, property and businesses in rural England and Wales.

It said farm reservoirs are "a crucial solution" to help farmers adapt to climate change as they store water from wetter winters and sudden downpours for use in irrigation during dry spells.

Building a farm reservoir needs planning consent, an abstraction licence to take water from a watercourse as well as funding.

The CLA said "too often, farm reservoir projects face lengthy approval processes that add delay, cost, and uncertainty".

Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said farmers were being "blocked by outdated planning rules and a lack of proper support".

"We need a national call to store programme right now - identifying where that capacity exists, removing the barriers, and backing farmers who want to be part of the solution," he said.

"The demands of our changing climate will not wait for Whitehall to catch up."

The government has promised a new round of funding for farm reservoirs will open in Autumn this year.

A Defra spokesperson said: "One of the Prime Minister's first visits was meeting farmers hit by brutal drought and dry weather, announcing a £65m package to help them through these challenging conditions, including £15m to support the development of on-farm reservoirs."

It said the £15m could support around 100 farms and if demand was greater, it would consider making more money available.

The government said it was also looking at changing planning rules and speeding up licensing for abstraction.

But Somerset farmer Philip Vaux said £15m was a "drop in the ocean".

CLA president Gavin Lane said the money was "a welcome and pragmatic move, but little more than a temporary fix".

"It will not change the reality that farming remains exceptionally difficult in this business environment, and in a country that does not have a plan for climate change adaption," he said.

Meanwhile, the National Farmers Union has called for the government to expand tax relief to include on-farm reservoirs in October's Budget.

articles.title: After Google renames 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' in the US; CEO Sundar Pichai says no to US government's request on changing name of Atlantic Ocean; tells: No, no, no, this time I'm not doing it as …

articles.body: President Trump, who floated the idea of renaming ‘Atlantic Ocean’ to ‘Trump Ocean’ earlier this month, has once again raised the possibility of renaming the ocean. Speaking at an event recently, Trump revealed that he called Google Maps and asked to rename the Atlantic Ocean. He said that Google CEO Sundar Pichai replied to his proposal saying: “No, no, no. This time I'm not doing it.” According to Trump, Pichai said, “Oceans are different, sir. They cover a lot of countries. Please don't ask us to do that.” This comes months after Google renamed 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' in the US following an executive order signed by Trump.Trump wants to rename ‘Atlantic Ocean’ to ‘Trump Ocean’As mentioned above, Trump first discussed renaming the Atlantic Ocean this month. “We’ve got the gulf. We’ve got a beautiful lake,” Trump said during a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee. “Now, somebody said, you need a river. We need a river. We need an ocean.”He jokingly said that the new name could be in honor of him. “We call it ‘Trump Ocean’ or ‘Ocean of the Americas,’ something like that,” Trump said further adding “Before I get out, I think we should have an ocean. And we need a great river.”US previously renamed Gulf of Mexico and Lake OntarioEarlier this month, the US administration renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, sparking diplomatic tensions between the US and Mexico. In August, Trump also renamed Lake Ontario, between New York and Canada, as “Lake America”.After an executive order, Google posted a brief update on its Google Maps blog, noting that it follows the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) for its maps. This primarily means that the company has to rename Lake Ontario in Google Maps. Google's update on the name change also made it clear that the change will be only for Google Map users in the US. According to Google, those in the US will only see the new name, which is 'Lake of America'. Meanwhile, Canadians will continue to see the 'Lake Ontario' label. In the rest of the world, Lake Ontario will take precedence, but Lake America will also be there in parentheses. articles.title: EBay layoffs: Online marketplace to cut 1,000 jobs; CEO says in memo: 'Our strategy is ​working', as Ebay pushes into …
articles.summary: EBay is cutting about 1,000 jobs.
articles.body: ​EBay is cutting about 1,000 jobs. In a memo Reuters reviewed, the online marketplace’s CEO, Jamie Iannone, told employees it plans to eliminate about 9% of its workforce as it simplifies operations and redirects resources to faster-growing businesses. The recent cuts follow another round of layoffs in February, when EBay dismissed about 800 employees, representing 6% of its workforce. The latest restructuring comes as the company focuses on authenticated luxury goods, collectables and refurbished products as well as categories that attract enthusiasts looking for valuable or harder-to-find items.​In the memo seen by Reuters, Iannone wrote, “Our strategy is working,” adding that “continuing to capture the significant opportunity ahead requires us to make thoughtful choices about where we focus and invest.” His comments suggest EBay sees the layoffs as a reallocation of resources, not a change in its current strategy. The company's spokesman also confirmed the latest planned layoffs and said affected employees should expect to receive notifications in the coming days. The company had 12,300 employees at the end of last year, before its two rounds of workforce reductions.​​Why EBay is cutting jobs despite its share gains​To distinguish itself from larger online retailers, EBay is focusing on categories where product condition, authenticity, and scarcity influence purchasing decisions, the Reuters report noted. Its authentication services matter most for luxury goods, sneakers, and collectables, where buyers may worry about counterfeits.​That strategy has helped Ebay shares gain nearly 40% this year, compared with about a 12% increase in the S&P 500. Its stock rose about 1% in early trading after the layoffs were confirmed.​The reductions are intended to simplify operations and shift spending toward faster-growing areas. However, Ebay has not provided a detailed breakdown of which teams or locations will be most affected.​Depop deal expands Ebay’s resale business​Ebay has also expanded its position in the resale market through its $1.4 billion acquisition of fashion platform Depop. The deal gave the company greater access to younger shoppers and increased its exposure to re-commerce, the resale of previously owned products.​The company’s recent performance allowed it to forecast third-quarter revenue above Wall Street estimates when it reported results in August. It is scheduled to release its latest earnings next week.​Ebay’s strategy has also attracted acquisition interest. GameStop CEO Ryan Cohen made an unsolicited $56 billion offer in May. articles.title: Saving scheme to set aside £10 a week for children in care
articles.summary: Eligible people in the care system will be able to access the savings once they turn 18.
articles.body:
A new government savings scheme will set aside £10 a week for children in care for them to access when they turn 18.

Established by the States' Children and Family Community Services and Guernsey Community Savings, it is designed to give young people a financial foundation when becoming an adult.

The States said the scheme will apply to children from entry into the care system and 40 will benefit immediately.

Associate director of children services Lucy Cook said the savings accounts would support young people by "helping them to access opportunities that might otherwise be out of reach."

The States of Guernsey said the transition to independent living for people in care can bring "significant financial pressures, from setting up a home to managing everyday living costs".

"Having savings of their own can offer greater choice, security and confidence as they take this important step," it said.

The States will pay a one-off fee to allpay, a payment services company, to establish the scheme.

The charity Guernsey Community Savings will then open and manage the accounts, and work with each young person and their social worker as they approach their 18th birthday.

At 18 years old, they will have the choice of opening an account with Guernsey Community Savings or transferring their savings to an account of their choice.

Cook said children in care deserve the opportunity to "look ahead with confidence and hope for their future".

"This initiative is about giving our care-experienced young people a stronger foundation and recognising our commitment to them as corporate parents.

"We want every child in care to know that they are valued, supported and encouraged to achieve their full potential."

Chief executive of Guernsey Community Savings Joe Brown said children from care are "particularly vulnerable to financial exclusion when they reach adulthood".

"Giving them the opportunity to build up savings, and the financial security that comes with this, can make a real difference as they take their first steps towards independence."

articles.title: Can Russia broker a new US-Iran deal?
articles.summary: Russia’s nuclear expertise, close ties with Tehran and negotiation experience could give Moscow an edge as a mediator.
articles.body:
This week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov travelled to Iran, where he met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and several other officials. The visit came on the tail of two meetings between Pezeshkian and Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 8 and September 1.

Media reports have indicated that Moscow has offered to mediate between Washington and Tehran in talks on a possible nuclear deal. Whether these efforts will be successful is too early to judge, but there are several factors that could make Russia a potentially more effective mediator than others.

As a major nuclear power and with state-owned nuclear energy giant Rosatom being a leader in the world’s civilian nuclear energy field, Russia is eminently competent in all aspects of the Iranian nuclear programme.

Moscow’s general attitude towards that programme has been clear. It supports Iranian ambition to have domestic nuclear energy generation; it is currently building two new units of the nuclear power plant in Bushehr. But it opposes Iranian development or acquisition of nuclear weapons. It certainly doesn’t want nuclear proliferation so close to its borders.

Furthermore, Russia’s relations with Iran, long testy, have markedly improved recently. One of the reasons for the growing trust between the two countries has been that both have been attacked by the United States: directly in the case of Iran and indirectly, in a proxy war fashion, in the case of Russia.

In 2022, Washington openly set the goal of “inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia”. Then, Iran came to Russia’s aid and transferred to Russia its Shahed drone technology.

In early 2025, the two countries signed the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, which outlined the parameters of expanding economic, political and military cooperation. It is important to note that the Russians proposed a mutual military assistance clause to include in the treaty, but the Iranians demurred.

Thus the criticism that Moscow supposedly failed to come to Tehran’s defence in the 12-day war of 2025 and in the ongoing military conflict is ill-informed. Russia has stood by Iran and has repaid its debt.

Helping the US reach a new nuclear deal with Iran would be clearly in Russia’s interest. Although Russia sees Iran as the true victor because of its stunning resilience in the face of the US-Israeli attacks, it also realises the enormity of the damage inflicted on its partner. Russia hopes that peace would unlock its major logistical project, the International North-South Transport Corridor to India, which passes through Iran.

Moscow also sees the Arab Gulf monarchies as important and useful allies and doesn’t want to jeopardise relations with them because of Iran’s retaliatory strikes against their territories. Even if Russia has gained financially due to the surge in oil prices as a result of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, these gains are of short duration. The continuing blockade is not in its interest.

Moscow is also in a strong position to mediate with Iran because it was part of the eight-party talks that led to the 2015 signing of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) addressing Iran’s nuclear programme.

Of those eight, the US withdrew while France, Germany, the United Kingdom and the European Union lost their standing in both Washington and Tehran because of their actions.

This essentially leaves US President Donald Trump with Russia and China. Russia, for its part, has already stepped up mediation efforts. This month, Putin reportedly delivered an Iranian proposal by phone to Trump. In parallel, there is heightened US diplomatic activity to bring an end to the war in Ukraine, where Trump for the first time is applying pressure on Kiev.

Meanwhile, the US president has mentioned that an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next month would make sense if it were focused on denuclearisation.

It is important to remember that the crises in Eurasia – from Ukraine to Iran and Taiwan – are intrinsically linked because they involve the principal geopolitical and military players of today’s world: the US, China and Russia.

The fact that for the first time ever the leaders of these three countries are discussing the possibility of a trilateral meeting is more than just a topic for pundits to mull on air.

This may not be the dawn of a new world order, but it could be a small step to balance wars with diplomacy.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
articles.summary: The bank says it is using more AI leading to a 5% reduction in its workforce.
articles.body:
Barclays is cutting its staff by around 5,000 as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes.

The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce.

The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall.

Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy.

The banking group is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected.

Barclays also revealed it made £2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast.

Economists have been watching companies' results carefully for signs that investment in new technology, and AI specifically, is making a difference in their day-to-day operations, leading to greater efficiency and lower employment.

Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business.

"AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future.

"We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake.

"Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI."

Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said Barclays was "reaching for the AI lever, expecting to cut a decent chunk of its workforce as it expands the use of artificial intelligence", but had failed to match expectations with its financial results.

Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years".

"Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said.

Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further £1.1bn of savings in 2027.

articles.title: In 2020, Edwin Wiek spent four days in a chimp’s former cage; by day four, donors had given €20,855 toward a Thai rescue centre caring for 780 animals
articles.summary: Edwin Wiek spent four days in a chimp's old cage to raise funds for Wildlife Friends Foundation Thailand during the pandemic, highlighting the plight of wildlife rescue centers.
articles.body: The media rarely cover wildlife rescue centres until an incident occurs. The majority of them survive on a consistent supply of volunteers, visitors, and small donations. But that support dried up quickly when Thailand’s tourism industry was hit by the pandemic in 2020. Edwin Wiek responded in July 2020 by spending four days in a cage in Bangkok where a chimpanzee named Canoe had previously been kept for more than 20 years, according to a 2015 report from the Wildlife Friends Foundation Thailand. Despite this, the animals continued to require daily sustenance. The rescue centre he established in Phetchaburi province, in which he was then caring for 780 animals, had received €20,855 in donations by the fourth day of his stay.Wildlife Friends Foundation Thailand is managed by Wiek, who was 54 years old at the time and is of Dutch descent. The rules, as outlined by WFFT, were stringent when he entered the cage at noon on Friday, July 10, 2020. He could only leave for the toilet six times a day, and he was prohibited from leaving for more than ten minutes at a time. The foundation's objective was to raise funds to nourish the wild animals under its care and to raise awareness of the millions of wild animals that are kept in cages as pets or tourist attractions.Life in the cageThe cage was small by any measure. Khaosod English reported that the cage measured 1.4 metres by 2.3 metres, with a ceiling just under two metres. "The mosquitoes, the ants and the snakes, I don't mind so much, but the lack of space does, and by the fourth day it was getting to me," Wiek told the paper. He also said that the chimpanzee that used to live there stayed in the same space for many days, putting his own time there in perspective.The fundraising process resembled a reality show. Viewers could pay to make Wiek's stay easier or more difficult while he was live-streamed on Facebook and YouTube. A 10-minute shower cost $200, while snacks and soft drinks started at $25. On the unfriendly side, it cost $250 to be hosed down, $300 to be poked with a bamboo stick, and $200 to have noise blasted at the cage for 15 minutes. Anyone willing to pay $5,000 could effectively throw away the key. According to Wiek, the majority of the donations came from Australia, the United States, and Europe. One challenge, wearing Thai-style clothing and a wig, was cut short to an hour because of the heat, according to Smart Local Thailand.The chimp who resided thereThe chimp was named Canoe. VICE World News reported that Canoe had already been moved to the rescue centre earlier in 2020, before Wiek's fundraising stay in the chimpanzee's former cage. His stay in Bangkok had been long and grim. WFFT reported in February 2015 that he had lived in a cage of roughly five square metres at a school in Bangkok for more than 20 years. On February 18 that year, Wiek sent a petition with 25,000 signatures to the head of Thailand’s Department of National Parks and Wildlife.Two days later, officials arrived with a court order and found the chimpanzee, a gibbon and a macaque kept under improper conditions. The gibbon and the macaque had ownership documents. Canoe didn’t, and the owner said he had kept him before Thailand’s wildlife laws came into effect. The foundation also pointed out that chimpanzees are a protected species under CITES, raising the question of how he had ever gotten into the country in the first place. Authorities instead recommended giving the animals to a rescue facility, and the owners were given 90 days to improve conditions to international standards.Where the money wentThe goal was $25,000. Different reports quote it in dollars and in euros, but they agree on the number. Khaosod English reported that donations had reached €20,855 by Monday, July 13, the fourth day of the fundraiser. Later coverage put the final total at between $25,000 and $30,000, enough to keep the centre operating for about a month, according to VICE World News.That sounds small until you see what the foundation was up against. In interviews during the pandemic, Wiek described a sharp fall in revenue after tourism and visitor numbers collapsed. He warned that the centre’s savings could run out within six to eight weeks and that facilities without income were beginning to consider giving their animals away. He warned the savings would be used up in six to eight weeks, and zoos and animal attractions with no income were beginning to think about giving their animals away. Wiek also warned that zoo closures and the loss of tourism revenue were putting additional pressure on animal facilities. By late 2020, the centre’s animal count had reportedly risen from 780 to roughly 850.The residents included gibbons, macaques, orangutans, chimpanzees, elephants and a bear. The Wildlife Friends Foundation says its rescue centre has taken in thousands of animals since it opened, many of them rescued from the pet trade, tourist photo props and entertainment attractions. Animals that cannot be released back into the wild remain in the centre’s care.Wiek later said he would undertake the fundraising stunt again, linking the pandemic to the wildlife exploitation his foundation had been fighting for 19 years. The campaign drew attention to the pressures facing rescue centres when tourism and visitor revenue disappear. Such facilities rely on donations as well as visitor income, and Wiek used his four days in Canoe’s former cage to highlight the consequences of keeping wild animals confined.You use AI every day. articles.title: BioWare: Mass Effect and Dragon Age video game studio to close
articles.summary: The influential studio that made Mass Effect and Dragon Age announces it is closing its doors.
articles.body:
BioWare, the video game studio behind sci-fi epic Mass Effect and fantasy saga Dragon Age, has been closed down.

The Canadian developer specialising in role-playing games was founded in 1995 and found millions of fans with its complex, branching narratives.

Its last two releases, however, did not meet sales expectations, and parent company Electronic Arts (EA) announced it had decided to close the studio as it cut 400 jobs across the business.

In its own statement, BioWare, which was working on a new Mass Effect game, thanked players for "being the most important part of the story" during its 31-year history.

The developer's first big taste of success came in 1998 when it released role-playing game Baldur's Gate, based on Dungeons and Dragons rules.

It became renowned for the quality of its games and in the late 2000s had twin successes with the Mass Effect trilogy and several Dragon Age games.

Mass Effect in particular is regarded as having a long-lasting influence on the video game industry thanks to its ambitious narrative and inclusion of same-sex relationships.

As industry trends changed, BioWare pivoted from single player to multiplayer games with the release of Anthem in 2019 - which disappointed fans and critics.

It followed up with Dragon Age: The Veilguard, the fourth game in the series, in 2024.

The game's protracted development cycle was blamed for its lukewarm reviews - particularly from long-time series fans, who complained it lacked the complex moral choices of its prequels.

Despite BioWare's recent performance, there was a huge response to the news.

Actors Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer, who voiced female and male versions of Mass Effect's main character Commander Shepherd, reacted via a livestream on Instagram.

Addressing fans, Hale said the community that had formed around the game would keep it alive.

"BioWare lives on. Mass Effect lives on. We live on," she said.

The pair closed the livestream by delivering Shepherd's famous line: "I should go on."

Fellow industry figures also showed their support for BioWare.

Michał Nowakowski, co-CEO of The Witcher developer CD Projekt Red, said BioWare had been "a massive part" of the Polish studio's history, "sharing their wisdom" since working to release Baldur's Gate in Eastern Europe.

"Not a great day in the games industry," he wrote .

BioWare project director Mike Gamble thanked fans and colleagues for the " words of support for the studio, the legacy, and the impact that BioWare has had on you".

The studio's closure comes months after EA - the video game giant responsible for series including EA FC, The Sims and Battlefield - was bought for $55bn by a Saudi Arabia-led group of investors .

As part of the deal, EA took on $20bn in debt, which the company will have to pay back.

In a message to staff, since published on its website , the company said it had taken a "hard look" at its business and chosen to focus on key titles and series.

This meant working on "fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects in the action-adventure space", it said, confirming that a new Iron Man game and a Star Wars Jedi title were being worked on.

The company said it had two projects in development under its EA Sports banner, including a "social-first" American Football game code-named "Project Gridiron", and that it was in the early stages of resurrecting boxing simulator Fight Night.

EA also said it was committed to the long-term success of skateboarding simulator Skate, and The Sims.

However, it did announce the cancellation of one new Sims project, and said there would be job cuts at Skate developer Full Circle.

The company said BioWare was "a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly".

articles.title: In 1926, an Atlanta woman donated her home to establish an art museum; 100 years later, the High Museum covers more than 300,000 square feet and is approaching 50,000 members as the city celebrates its centennial
articles.summary: A century ago, a private home on Peachtree Street became the starting point for what would grow into one of the American South’s most significant cultural
articles.body: A century ago, a private home on Peachtree Street became the starting point for what would grow into one of the American South’s most significant cultural institutions. Today, the High Museum of Art stretches across more than 300,000 square feet, houses a collection of over 20,000 works and is nearing 50,000 members, reflecting a remarkable transformation that has unfolded alongside Atlanta itself.As the city celebrates the museum’s centennial, the High is marking the occasion not simply by revisiting its history, but by looking at how art can continue to shape the city’s cultural future.From a Peachtree Street home to a major museumAccording to the High Museum of Art, the institution was established in October 1926, when Mrs. Hattie High donated her stately Peachtree Street residence to Atlanta for use as a school and museum. The gesture came during a period when cultural leaders in the rapidly developing city were beginning to see the arts as an important part of public life.Over the following century, that original vision expanded dramatically. The High evolved from a modest regional institution into a major cultural hub for the Southeast, with collections spanning centuries, continents and mediums. Its holdings also include significant works by Southern artists, reflecting the region’s complex artistic history.The centennial programme builds on that legacy with new exhibitions, collection displays, acquisitions, partnerships and community initiatives.A museum increasingly shaped by its cityThe High’s centennial celebrations have taken art outside the traditional museum experience. Georgia Public Broadcasting (GPB) reported on the museum’s Centennial Community Block Party, where hundreds of people gathered for live music, food trucks and interactive art as Atlanta marked the milestone.The museum has also planned a series of events throughout October, including free admission, walking tours, teen programming and seasonal celebrations. These initiatives reflect a broader shift in how the High engages with its audience.According to the High Museum of Art, visitors of colour accounted for 55% of attendance in recent years, up from 15% in 2015. Younger audiences have also become an increasingly important part of the institution’s community, while free admission programmes and after-hours events have helped broaden access.That transformation is visible in the museum’s membership as well. GPB reports that membership has grown from fewer than 25,000 a decade ago to just a few hundred short of 50,000 today.Reimagining the collection for the next centuryThe centennial year brings substantial changes inside the museum, too. The High is reinstalling its American and African Art galleries, moving towards thematic and material connections rather than purely chronological displays, states the GPB report.The new presentations will introduce significant acquisitions, including a rare Jacob Lawrence painting, a quilt by Carolyn L. Mazloomi and a work by Grandma Moses. The African galleries will feature works by artists including Ben Enwonwu, Ladi Kwali, Nike Okundaye, Bruce Onobrakpeya and Jimoh Akolo, also adds GPB report.The museum is also adding more than 200 works across photography, contemporary art and design, while a commemorative publication will trace the institution’s century-long journey.Beyond its walls, partnerships with MARTA, the Atlanta Beltline, Atlanta Hawks, UPS, Delta Air Lines and other organisations will bring art into different corners of the city.The next 100 yearsAtlanta’s cultural landscape has expanded considerably since the High first opened its doors. With the city now recognised as a major centre for music, film and visual arts, the museum enters its second century amid a broader creative renaissance.Its centennial, therefore, is more than a birthday. It is a marker of how far Atlanta’s cultural ambitions have travelled, from one donated home in 1926 to an institution increasingly defined by its collections, its audiences and its place in the life of the city.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and Instagram/highmuseuamofartYou use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Rahul Gandhi, Raihan Vadra’: BJP takes 'launch' jibe as photo exhibition row escalates
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The controversy over the removal of photographs from artist Raihan Vadra’s exhibition at Bikaner House has escalated into a political
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The controversy over the removal of photographs from artist Raihan Vadra’s exhibition at Bikaner House has escalated into a political confrontation, with BJP national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia targeting the Gandhi family and accusing it of focusing on regaining power.Speaking about the row, Bhatia took aim at Congress leaders who had backed Raihan, the son of Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and businessman Robert Vadra. He alleged that the family was seeking to position Raihan for a political role.“Congress' psychophant leaders are saying that he is the future president of Congress. One defective product who has lost 99 elections has not been launched by Sonia mummy. Now Priyanka mummy's mission has come to launch Raihan,” Bhatia said, as quoted by ANI.Continuing his attack, the BJP spokesperson accused the Gandhi family of being willing to do anything to return to power.“This fake Gandhi family wants power every time, and as soon as they are out of power, they will do anything. They can do anything for power. The law will prevail in the country, be it the defective product Rahul Gandhi or the future president of Congress, Raihan Vadra. Priyanka mummy is now on a new mission. After the launch of Rahul Gandhi, Raihan will be launched,” he added.Raihan questions restrictions on artistic expressionThe BJP's remarks came amid a dispute over Raihan's exhibition, titled No Idea Is Fine, at Bikaner House in New Delhi. Raihan had alleged that the venue's management objected to photographs documenting youth protests in Delhi and instructed him to remove images featuring the Indian Tricolour.Speaking about the decision, Raihan said he did not know whether there had been pressure from elsewhere but believed the decision had been taken by the venue's management.“I don't know if there was any pressure or anything from anywhere else. I know that it was the management here that decided to, take that decision,” he said, according to ANI.Raihan also said he was unsure whether the decision had been politically motivated. However, he argued that public institutions and major art fairs had a responsibility to protect the interests of artists, galleries and curators.“Those people have to be responsible and they cannot put a curb on our freedoms of expression as artists. just because it doesn't suit them. You know, tomorrow if there are different people in charge here and they remove something, it's wrong,” he said.“Any curtailment of remunerative expression and art is wrong. any form of censorship is wrong,” he added.According to an earlier account by Raihan, the exhibition was scheduled to open at 7 pm, but Bikaner House officials raised objections to the photographs shortly before the event. He alleged that officials eventually insisted that all 70 images be removed, citing the venue's policy on political content.Raihan said he had shared the exhibition layout a week in advance and questioned why the objections had not been raised earlier. He also alleged that officials did not provide written explanations for the removal of individual photographs.He said the management issued a notice warning that the building would be sealed and the exhibition cancelled if the photographs were not removed by 5 pm. Raihan subsequently turned the frames around, before moving them into storage after officials objected to that arrangement as well.The dispute also involved two photographs of the national flag. Raihan said he asked the officials to provide a written order directing him to remove them but did not receive one.Priyanka, Robert Vadra back artistRaihan's mother, Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, had publicly supported him amid the controversy.In a post on X, she wrote: “@raihanrvadra. When someone with power becomes afraid of the expression of another, he doesn’t know it, but he has already lost the very power he is trying to protect. You stand for what is true and everything beautiful will find its way to you. I am proud of you, always will be.”Robert Vadra also shared his son's statement about the exhibition.Congress leaders separately criticised the reported removal of the photographs. Congress MP Karti Chidambaram described the Bikaner House administration's behaviour as “Absolutely churlish & obtuse”, while Congress Rajya Sabha MP Pawan Khera alleged that the episode amounted to censorship.Raihan had earlier said the exhibition would continue in a limited capacity while he looked for an alternative venue to display the complete collection.The exhibition is also scheduled to be held in Bengaluru next month.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1896, William Morris produced an illustrated Chaucer book with 87 woodcuts; one of roughly 50 copies given a rare luxury binding, it retained its original case and sold for Rs 2.68 crore in October 2026
articles.summary: A book printed more than 130 years ago has drawn attention for its remarkable craftsmanship and rarity.
articles.body: A book printed more than 130 years ago has drawn attention for its remarkable craftsmanship and rarity. 'The Works of Geoffrey Chaucer', an illustrated edition produced by British designer and printer William Morris in 1896, reportedly sold for Rs 2.68 crore in October 2026. Known as the Kelmscott Chaucer, the volume is celebrated for combining mediaeval literature with intricate printing, elaborate illustrations and an extraordinary binding.What makes this copy particularly special is that it retains its original white pigskin binding, designed by Morris, along with its original chemise and clamshell storage box made by the Doves Bindery. According to the Christie's catalogue, approximately 50 copies of the book were commissioned in this deluxe binding, making it considerably rarer than the standard edition.The 1896 masterpiece that took years to createThe Kelmscott Chaucer was one of the most ambitious projects undertaken by Morris at his Kelmscott Press in Hammersmith, London. Morris, known for his contributions to the Arts and Crafts movement, believed that books should be beautiful objects as well as vehicles for literature. The project brought together his printing and decorative designs with illustrations by his longtime artistic collaborator, Edward Burne-Jones. Work on the book began several years before publication, with printing starting in August 1894. The completed volume was issued to subscribers in June 1896.The edition contained 87 large woodcut illustrations based on Burne-Jones's drawings. These were redrawn by Robert Catterson-Smith and engraved on wood by W. H. Hooper. Morris also designed the decorative borders, ornamental initials, title page and other elements that give the book its distinctive appearance. The book was printed in black and red using specially designed typefaces, including Chaucer type and Troy type. Its pages feature elaborate borders, decorative frames and large initial words, reflecting Morris's attention to detail. The original edition comprised 438 copies, including 425 printed on paper and 13 on vellum, according to Christie's catalogue.Why the rare pigskin binding makes this copy specialAlthough the book itself is highly regarded, its binding adds another layer of historical and artistic significance. Morris designed a special white pigskin binding inspired by German bookbinding traditions of the 15th century. The covers feature intricate blind tooling, including grapevine patterns, roses, fleur-de-lys and oak-leaf motifs. The lower cover is divided into decorative geometric panels, while the spine has five compartments, and the book closes with two metal clasps.The design was influenced by historic bindings in Morris's own library, including a 1478 Bible associated with the Salzburg binder Ulrich Schreier. The result combines mediaeval decorative influences with Morris's distinctive approach to book design. The Doves Bindery executed the binding, and the catalogue identifies this particular copy as one of approximately 50 specially bound examples. The traditional count of these bindings has been 48, although bibliographical research suggests that additional copies were bound later.The book also comes with its original chemise and clamshell box. The leather-covered box was made over an oak structure, with a lined interior and a brass hinge and concealed clasp. Although the case has some wear and its locking mechanism is defective, retaining these original accessories adds to the copy's historical interest.A collector's item valued for more than its ageThe Kelmscott Chaucer has long been admired by book collectors, historians and design enthusiasts. Its importance lies not simply in its age but in the collaboration between Morris and Burne-Jones and the extraordinary care taken in its production. The University of Maryland Libraries describes the book as the culmination of Morris's vision for an ideal book, while Trinity College Dublin highlights its place among the most ornate productions of the Kelmscott Press.The reported sale price of Rs 2.68 crore reflects the interest surrounding this exceptionally bound copy. However, the value of rare books can vary significantly depending on their condition, provenance, binding, completeness and the presence of original accessories. For collectors, this edition represents a meeting point between literature, printing history and decorative art. More than a century after its publication, the Kelmscott Chaucer continues to demonstrate how a printed book can become an enduring work of art.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ‘Anti-Indian hate is exploding’: US lawmaker Raja Krishnamoorthi accuses big tech firms of profiting from online hatred
articles.summary: Indian-origin US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi demands accountability from major tech firms for profiting from a surge of anti-Indian and anti-South Asian hatred on social media platforms, urging Congress to intervene.
articles.body: Indian-origin US Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi has accused major technology companies of benefiting from anti-Indian, anti-Hindu and anti-South Asian hatred on social media, arguing that the platforms are profiting from the spread of online hate while having little incentive to stop it.In a X post, he wrote: “Anti-Indian hate is exploding on social media, and Big Tech is profiting from it. These companies have no incentive to stop the hatred they help spread. Congress must hold them accountable.”His remarks follow a September report by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH), which documented a rise in online hostility towards South Asian communities in the United States. Researchers identified approximately 542,360 hateful posts targeting South Asians on X between January 2025 and June 2026. articles.title: Skegness sea air damaging Jolly Fisherman artwork
articles.summary: The town council is spending £2,500 on conservation work to prevent further deterioration.
articles.body:
"Irreplaceable" artwork depicting the Jolly Fisherman skipping on Skegness beach has deteriorated because of exposure to the sea air, the town council has been told.

The mascot was first painted by John Hassall for a poster campaign advertising the resort in 1908.

The blue pigment on Jolly's jumper and the sea have darkened over time in two paintings now owned by the town council.

The town clerk said the paint has been affected by a "chemical reaction to the sea air" but that the council had commissioned work to prevent "further deterioration".

The two paintings, which are 101 and 118 years old have been on display at the Tower Gardens Pavilion in the town since being restored in 2020.

The original Jolly Fisherman poster, which features the slogan "Skegness is so bracing", was commissioned by the Great Northern Railway to encourage visitors to take the train on their seaside breaks to the town.

The artwork was gifted to the town council by the Great Northern Railway company in 1966.

A report to Skegness Town Council by Museum Conservation Services said "irreversible" changes to the pigments have been caused by a combination of "light, moisture and chlorine".

At a meeting of the Town Council's management committee on 21 October it was agreed to spend £2500 on specialist work to "stop further deterioration" of the paintings.

But it stopped short of approving work which would involve restoring the colours "because it was felt the painting would be changed" by the process.

Local artist John Byford said the damage was "incredibly worrying" and was concerned about the "the conditions in which these paintings have been displayed".

He was unconvinced the blame lay on the "bracing sea air", pointing to galleries based in other seaside resorts like the Tate in St Ives and the Turner Contemporary on the seafront in Margate, "I don't buy it," he added.

He said the "south facing, hot" cafe in the building was "not an environment for important works of art".

"Our heritage is irreplaceable," he said, adding that he hoped there would be "better protection for these precious artworks".

A spokesperson from the town council said it "completely rejects that it's not been taking care of the paintings".

They also added that it "considers it really important that residents in Skegness see them, because they're part of the town's history".

articles.title: Claims 'stabbed' Eleanor Barnfield tried to drive to hospital due to ambulance wait denied
articles.summary: Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to a crash in Bridgend on Monday.
articles.body:
The Welsh Ambulance Service has denied that a woman who died after crashing a car into a wall after suffering "stab wounds" was driving because of ambulance wait times.

Eleanor Barnfield, 47, died in hospital after police were called to the crash in Bridgend on Monday, where they found she had "puncture wounds unrelated to the collision", which the BBC understands were sustained in a stabbing.

A 61-year-old man from Bridgend, who has been arrested on suspicion of murder, remains in custody.

The ambulance service said it was aware of "misleading rumours" circulating online but said medics were called to the crash in Coity Road at about 12:44 BST and a response unit arrived seven minutes later.

Reports in some media had claimed Eleanor had crashed her car while driving herself to hospital.

In a statement about the crash, the ambulance service said two emergency ambulances arrived after the response unit to provide additional support at 13:07 and 13:13.

It described the rumours on social media as "contradictory" and "factually untrue".

"We would encourage members of the public not to speculate," the service said.

It also confirmed that "advanced critical care" was delivered by the emergency medical retrieval and transfer service, which arrived by helicopter, before the patient was driven to hospital.

South Wales Police said it made the arrest on Tuesday after undergoing a "significant" police operation at a retirement housing complex, Ger-y-Nant, near the crash.

Eleanor worked for the housing association Valleys to Coast, which runs the complex that provides accommodation for over-60s and consists of 13 flats.

In a family tribute on Wednesday, Eleanor was described by her family as the " kindest, most loving, bravest person in the world".

"She meant everything to us and will be forever loved and missed deeply by her devoted family and friends. She was our rock," the tribute added.

Jo Oak, chief executive of Valleys to Coast, said Eleanor was a "much-valued member" of the team and they were "devastated" by her loss.

Oak added the organisation would "continue to cooperate fully with South Wales Police".

Police have thanked the patience and support of residents and said communities may notice an "increased police presence" as the investigation continues.

articles.title: In 1926, Frankfurt began installing the world's first modern fitted kitchens in thousands of homes; a century later, most are gone, but volunteers have saved parts from about 50 as a new preservation effort takes shape
articles.summary: In 1926, Frankfurt began installing a new kind of kitchen in its homes.
articles.body: In 1926, Frankfurt began installing a new kind of kitchen in its homes. Designed by Austrian architect Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky, the compact, fitted kitchen used built-in cupboards, worktops and carefully arranged storage to make cooking more efficient. About 10,000 were installed across the German city. A century later, most have disappeared, but volunteers are salvaging surviving fittings and restoring some kitchens in their original homes. As reported by Architectural Digest, parts from around 50 Frankfurt Kitchens have been rescued and stored in a warehouse, as conservation specialists work to preserve the design that helped shape the modern fitted kitchen.How the Frankfurt Kitchen changed home designThe Frankfurt Kitchen was designed as part of ‘Neues Frankfurt,’ a municipal housing programme launched to address the housing shortage after World War I. Architect and urban planner Ernst May led the programme, and Schütte-Lihotzky joined his team in 1925. She was tasked with designing a compact kitchen that could be produced at scale and reduce the time spent on household work. Inspired by railway dining-car kitchens and Taylorism, a system that studies work movements to improve efficiency, she arranged the stove, sink, storage and counters to minimise unnecessary steps.Measuring approximately 6.2 by 11.3 feet, the kitchen made use of nearly every available space. Shelves above the sink allowed dishes to drain, a removable drawer collected cooking waste, and an ironing board folded away beneath an adjustable ceiling lamp. Aluminium containers with handles and pouring spouts stored flour, sugar and other dry ingredients.The design included an electric stove, built-in cupboards, linoleum flooring and tiled backsplashes intended to make cleaning easier. Its original blue colour was chosen because it was believed to deter flies. By supplying fitted furniture as part of the apartment, the housing programme also reduced the need for residents to buy and arrange separate kitchen furnishings. According to the official website of The Victoria and Albert Museum, the Frankfurt Kitchen was the first fitted kitchen produced in mass quantities.A design focused on women's domestic workAs reported by Architectural Digest, Schütte-Lihotzky's design addressed a part of domestic life that architecture had often overlooked: the time and effort required to cook and manage a household. At the time, these tasks were largely treated as women's responsibilities. The kitchen brought them into the centre of architectural planning, aiming to make routine work more efficient. However, making domestic work more efficient did not change who was expected to do it. Steinberger noted that while the design made cooking and cleaning easier, “it didn’t change who was doing the work.”The kitchen's influence extended beyond Frankfurt. Its integration of storage, appliances and work surfaces helped establish a model that remains familiar in modern homes, even though materials and technology have changed.Why so few original kitchens remainMany Frankfurt Kitchens were removed as residents renovated their apartments or replaced old fittings. The Ernst-May-Gesellschaft, a nonprofit dedicated to preserving the city's architectural heritage, has spent years trying to save what remains. Volunteers are alerted when a historic apartment is due for renovation and its kitchen is at risk of being discarded. The society arranged to receive notifications about kitchens scheduled for removal. Its volunteers document each interior before dismantling it, photographing and measuring the room and recording the original fittings.The salvaged pieces are taken to a warehouse of approximately 2,150 square feet in Frankfurt-Fechenheim. There, conservators clean and restore cupboards, handles, screws, lampshades, floor tiles and other components. These pieces can later be used to reconstruct kitchens for museums and cultural institutions.Keeping the kitchens in their original homesPreservation efforts have also shifted towards restoring kitchens where they were originally installed. According to Architectural Digest, some historic housing estates and their interiors have received landmark protection, allowing selected kitchens to be repaired and retained in place.Conservator Kerstin Frost is working with architect Kristian Kaffenberger on these projects. The aim is to retain original cabinetry while making the kitchens practical for modern use. Updated versions can accommodate refrigerators, dishwashers, extra storage and higher counters. The original counters were around 31 inches high; restored versions are being raised to approximately 35 inches to suit contemporary needs.A century after Schütte-Lihotzky's design was first installed, preservationists are working to ensure that the Frankfurt Kitchen survives not only as a museum object but also as part of the city's living architectural history.You use AI every day. articles.title: Katie Price's ex-husband Kieran Hayler cleared of raping girl, 13
articles.summary: Kieran Hayler had denied rape, sexual assault and sexual activity with a child at his trial.
articles.body:
Katie Price's ex-husband, Kieran Hayler, has been found not guilty of raping a 13-year-old girl.

Hayler, 39, has been on trial accused of rape and sexual assault against the girl in West Sussex in 2016, when he was married to the media personality.

In total he was acquitted of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault at Lewes Crown Court.

Hayler had also faced four alternative counts of sexual activity with a child, for which he was also found not guilty.

He had denied the allegations, telling the jury that he believed them to be fabricated.

Price and Hayler separated in 2018, and later divorced in 2021.

Hayler had told the court that Price had "launched a campaign" against him after their marriage broke down, and that the allegations formed part of it.

He told the trial that "trust had gone on both sides" of his marriage to Price by mid-2013, and he admitted affairs with three other women during their relationship.

Giving evidence, Price denied being "angry and vengeful" towards her ex-husband.

The jury, made up of four men and six women, acquitted Hayler after 14 hours and 55 minutes of deliberations.

Hayler was emotional and bent over as he was discharged and told he could leave the dock.
