articles.title: France unrest: Macron vows ban on 'illegitimate' protests in coming days, blames 'seditious ultra-left'
articles.summary: French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday said \"illegitimate\" protests would be banned in the coming days, as authorities stepped up security measures
articles.body: French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday said "illegitimate" protests would be banned in the coming days, as authorities stepped up security measures ahead of another weekend of demonstrations following widespread riots and looting across the country.Macron also announced plans to convene a defence council meeting on Friday to review the security situation, with fresh protests expected over the weekend.Speaking after a meeting with intelligence officials, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and senior ministers, Macron said demonstrations organised by recognised groups, including trade unions, would be offered alternative routes to protect businesses from further damage. "France will bar protests that are not organised by unions in coming days," he said, as quoted by Reuters.The French president further blamed "seditious" ultra-left groups and vandals for the violence that swept across France last Saturday, when masked protesters clashed with police, looted shops and set vehicles on fire.His remarks came as authorities banned demonstrations planned for Thursday in several major cities, including Paris, Lyon, Lille and Grenoble, citing fears of renewed violence.In Paris, restrictions were imposed around sensitive locations, including the Elysee presidential palace, parliament buildings and major railway stations. The ban, effective until 8 pm local time, also covered central areas that suffered extensive damage during the weekend riots.The restrictions have raised concerns over the right to protest, even as the government maintains that tougher measures are necessary to prevent further destruction.Authorities are preparing for another major demonstration on Saturday, when activists associated with the "yellow vest" movement, which shook France with protests over fuel prices in 2018 and 2019, are expected to join the mobilisation.Lecornu, who met trade union representatives on Wednesday, said a "massive" security operation would be deployed to prevent a repeat of last weekend's violence.Union representatives, however, said the talks failed to produce concrete proposals to address their concerns. They are now preparing for another nationwide day of action on November 5, urging public and private sector employees to participate.How did the protests begin?The unrest began last month at a high school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, where students protested against staff shortages. The demonstrations soon spread to other Paris suburbs and eventually across France, with students organising class strikes, blockades and marches.Students have raised concerns over inadequate school funding, deteriorating infrastructure and teacher shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods. Some have also demanded changes to the university admissions system, which they consider complicated and unfair.What began as a student-led movement has since evolved into broader protests over the rising cost of living and dissatisfaction with the government's response to social and economic grievances.The unrest comes months before France's next presidential election, adding to the political pressure on his administration as it struggles to contain the demonstrations while addressing demands for reform.You use AI every day. articles.title: France reports first human Shamonda virus case, says no health risk
articles.summary: Until now, the virus was considered non-transferable to humans, making the patient the first documented human case.
articles.body:
French authorities have confirmed that a patient who died at a Lyon hospital earlier in October was infected with the Shamonda virus, the first such report of the virus in a human.

In a statement on Thursday, the French Ministry of Agriculture stressed that there were no identifiable health risks to the general population at this time.

Shamonda is an orthobunyavirus – a group of viruses primarily carried and spread by insects – transmitted to animals, mainly cattle, by biting midges of the genus Culicoides.

It was first detected in Nigeria in the 1960s, but has since been reported sporadically in East and Southern Africa, as well as Japan.

Until now, the virus was considered non-transmissible to humans, making the patient in France the first documented human case.

The French announcement said the leading hypothesis was that the patient was infected in eastern France, where the virus had circulated among animals this spring and summer.

“Clinical, biological and epidemiological investigations are continuing in conjunction with expertise in human, animal and environmental health,” the statement added.

Shamonda was first confirmed in Europe in late July after genomic tests on sick cattle in southern Germany, Switzerland and eastern France.

A report from France’s ‌weekly animal health surveillance bulletin said the virus had also been detected in Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain, and the United Kingdom’s Jersey.

articles.title: Celebrity Traitors producer 'amazed by reaction' to show
articles.summary: Stephen Lambert, from Studio Lambert, speaks to the BBC ahead of a talk in Oxford on Thursday.
articles.body:
With much of the country gripped by the latest series of The Celebrity Traitors, the man behind the show has told the BBC he has been "amazed by the reaction" to it.

Stephen Lambert is the chief executive of Studio Lambert - the company which has produced the programme, and its civilian version, for the BBC since 2022.

Alongside The Traitors, the production company is also responsible for hits including Race Across the World, Gogglebox and Squid Game: The Challenge.

The TV producer first started the company in 2008, and was speaking to BBC Radio Oxford ahead of an event at the city's Schwarzman Centre on Thursday evening.

Claudia Winkleman's Scottish murder-mystery game is currently on everyone's lips - although Lambert explained the format wasn't original to the UK.

"The Traitors was actually created by some brilliant Dutch people, who we then managed to get hold of the rights from to make the show in Britain and America," he said.

"Our brilliant team make those two versions and they've been hugely successful, so we've been amazed by the reaction."

The first UK series of The Traitors made it to screens in 2022, and proved an instant hit with TV audiences - all in an age of falling linear audiences.

That culminated in record nine million people tuning in live for the launch of The Celebrity Traitors earlier this month - all to see actor Richard E Grant make one of the game's biggest ever slip-ups .

Lambert said the appeal for the show came from "the melodrama of the whole thing, the cloaks, the talk of murder - it's all absurd but we enjoy the absurdity".

"I think the key thing is the game. The game is the engine of the whole show and it's based on what the Greeks called dramatic irony," he said.

"The fact that we the audience know more than the participants that we're watching... we know who they [the traitors] are."

"We find it very entertaining either watching them [the faithfuls] get it right and work out the traitors are, or it's often more entertaining seeing them get it wrong."

The first series of The Celebrity Traitors, which aired last year, saw one of the great upsets in reality TV history - as comedian Alan Carr emerged victorious at the final roundtable after the faithfuls failed to identify him as a traitor.

That was even after a series of faux paz throughout the series - including in the penultimate episode, when Carr could not keep a straight face whilst telling his other competitors that he was a faithful .

Audiences reacted with a mix of glee and astoundment at the comedian's triumph, with Lambert saying it was part of "the genius of the format".

"We the audience know who the traitors are right from the beginning, we see them being picked, and that completely changes the dynamics of the viewing experience."

In a country where lying on reality television can turn people into public enemy number one, Lambert said the fact that the audience were constantly in on the ruse enhanced the format.

"The fact the traitors are licenced to lie means that, just like a good poker player, we are impressed by their ability to be traitors - rather than thinking 'oh this is revealing a kind of terrible character flaw'."

"In other reality shows you sometimes feel that you don't really like a person because they're lying, but in in The Traitors you have no worries about that."

articles.title: What is the Turkiye-Libya maritime deal, and why are the EU, Egypt opposed?
articles.summary: Eastern Libya’s parliament backs a sea border pact with Ankara, a shift that analysts say redraws Libya’s alliances.
articles.body:
Libya’s eastern-based parliament has backed a 2019 maritime deal with Turkiye already signed by the North African nation’s internationally recognised government based in Tripoli to delimit maritime boundaries in the Mediterranean Sea.

The vote on Tuesday came as Turkiye has been cultivating close ties in recent years with the eastern parliament, backed by renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar. Ankara had helped the Tripoli government, known as the Government of National Accord (GNA), push back an offensive in 2020 by Haftar’s self-styled Libyan National Army (LNA) that aimed to capture Tripoli.

Egypt and the European Union have rejected the ratification of the maritime borders agreement, calling the deal “null and void”.

On Tuesday, the Tobruk-based House of Representatives voted unanimously to approve the agreement, reversing its 2020 rejection.

Israel also condemned the move while Greece, which said the agreement violates international law, briefed the United Nations Security Council.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan dismissed the criticism, calling the deal “entirely legitimate”.

So what is the deal, and why has it drawn such a backlash? Here’s what you need to know:

It is a memorandum of understanding that draws a sea border between Turkiye and Libya across the eastern Mediterranean.

It was signed in Istanbul on November 27, 2019, by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Fayez al-Sarraj, then-prime minister of the UN-recognised government in Tripoli.

Within weeks, Turkiye sent drones and military advisers to help repel Haftar’s assault on Tripoli.

The deal allowed Ankara to claim large and potentially gas-rich areas of the eastern Mediterranean.

Because Cairo says it cuts into Egyptian waters.

Egypt’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the agreement “constitutes a clear infringement upon Egypt’s sovereign rights within its exclusive economic zone and continental shelf”.

It said the ratification “carries no legal consequences for Egypt”.

President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has historically been one of Haftar’s strongest backers, but experts said their relations have cooled because Haftar allowed his territory to be used to funnel support to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group, which is fighting Sudan’s military, the AFP news agency reported.

Cairo is also now a close security ally of Ankara, and in July, Egypt refrained from objecting to a maritime line drawn between Benghazi and Turkiye.

According to exclusive information Al Jazeera received in July, the rapprochement between Ankara and Haftar’s general command included agreements on developing military facilities and advanced surveillance systems.

The agreements also included training programmes in Turkiye for eastern Libyan officers with specialised Turkish defence companies participating in the projects.

Wolfgang Pusztai, a security policy analyst and former Austrian defence attache in Greece, told Al Jazeera that a possible Turkish military presence in eastern Libya was “probably more of a concern for Egypt”.

“This is not so much an issue for Greece, which has a Turkish military presence next door anyway,” he said, adding, “I doubt Cairo would accept this.”

Because two of its member states said it seeks to take their waters.

In a joint statement on Tuesday, European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the memorandum infringes on the sovereign rights of third states and does not comply with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

They reaffirmed the bloc’s solidarity with Greece and Cyprus.

Athens said the deal ignores Greek islands, including Crete, Rhodes and Karpathos, and therefore infringes on its maritime territory, according to a briefing document from the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Sotirios Zartaloudis, an associate professor in comparative European politics at the University of Birmingham, told Al Jazeera that Athens and Nicosia see the deal as a Turkish attempt to block the “crucial Great Sea Interconnector”.

The planned subsea power cable, which would link Greece’s grid to Cyprus and later Israel, has been delayed by a dispute between Athens and Ankara over waters off the Greek island of Crete, the Reuters news agency reported last year. The project is estimated to cost about $2.1bn.

Turkiye has not signed UNCLOS, which means Ankara is not bound by the treaty’s rules governing maritime boundaries.

On Wednesday, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas urged all countries to respect member states’ sovereign rights under EU and international law, including UNCLOS.

Zartaloudis said both countries had pushed for the EU to condemn the deal, but “so far expectations were not met”, and that “they will try to gain further support against the deal”.

He added that “the main actor in the region is the US”, which he said had not repudiated the agreement.

Ankara said the deal is lawful and already in force.

Turkiye’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the memorandum safeguards both countries’ rights on the basis of international law and “the principle of equity”.

“There are countries reacting to this. We know why they are reacting,” Fidan told state media.

“However, this is an entirely legitimate deal, both from a legal and a statutory perspective,” he said.

Because Ankara has spent years courting it and its parliament has new leadership.

After Ankara struck a deal with Haftar’s LNA in July, the eastern parliament on October 6 elected Al-Salhin Abdelnabi al-Obeidi as speaker, replacing Aguila Saleh after more than 12 years.

Al-Obeidi previously chaired the Libyan-Turkish parliamentary friendship committee.

Anas El Gomati, director of the Sadeq Institute, a Libyan think tank, told Al Jazeera that the turnaround in eastern Libya was about the route to the presidency under a US mediation plan for Saddam Haftar, Khalifa Haftar’s son and deputy commander.

“Turkiye is now the most consequential outside power in Libya with leverage over Tripoli and a military presence in the west, and he needs it to get there and to stay there,” El Gomati said.

“But a ratified treaty is hard to reverse, so Ankara gets something that looks permanent in return for support that, depending on how the Haftars use it, may not be,” El Gomati said.

Not on the issues that divide them most.

Tripoli’s GNU welcomed Tuesday’s vote, meaning both of Libya’s rival centres of power now back the deal.

But El Gomati said the “unification was never about the sea”.

“It’s about who controls the budget, the army and the electoral commission, and this vote touches none of them,” he said.

Athens said it would take all appropriate measures to safeguard its sovereign rights.

El Gomati said implementation now depended on institutions such as Libya’s National Oil Corporation and he expected pressure “to be diplomatic and slow”.

Pusztai said the risk of naval incidents if Turkiye or Libya act on the deal at sea was “very high”.

He said it might also lead to the involvement of the EU naval mission enforcing the UN arms embargo on Libya since 2020.

In August 2020, months after the deal was signed with the GNU, Ankara sent the survey vessel Oruc Reis to explore for oil and gas in waters Greece claims, bringing the two NATO allies to the verge of military confrontation.

articles.title: Pistol from Amritsar, delivered via ‘dead letter box’: Tiger Shroff murder bid revives concern over Pakistan-linked arms smuggling in Punjab
articles.summary: AMRITSAR: The alleged use of a pistol sourced from Amritsar in the October 18 firing at Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff’s car in Mumbai has brought Punjab’s
articles.body: AMRITSAR: The alleged use of a pistol sourced from Amritsar in the October 18 firing at Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff’s car in Mumbai has brought Punjab’s cross-border arms-smuggling routes under renewed security scrutiny. Intelligence and security agencies met on Thursday to assess the emerging threat and explore possible links between local weapon couriers, organised crime networks and Pakistan-based smugglers.Police probing the Mumbai firing have reportedly found that a pistol and 20 rounds of ammunition were collected from a pre-arranged location in Amritsar through a method known as a “dead letter box”, in which weapons are left at designated spots for recipients to collect without meeting the suppliers. The transfer was allegedly coordinated through an encrypted messaging application, and the weapon was subsequently transported to Mumbai, according to reports on the investigation.The development has raised concerns about how weapons smuggled into Punjab could be channelled into criminal networks operating in other parts of the country, even as security agencies continue to grapple with the cross-border smuggling of arms, ammunition and narcotics using drones.Border villages under scannerHighly placed security sources said several villages on the Pakistani side of the international border, particularly those within roughly three kilometres of it, were suspected of being used as launch sites for drone operations. The unmanned aerial vehicles reportedly travel five to seven kilometres into Indian territory to drop consignments at designated locations, where local handlers retrieve them.Intelligence inputs have identified several suspected smuggling points opposite Punjab’s border districts. These include Rohilla and Tejeke opposite Fazilka; Gatti Kalanjar opposite Ferozepur; Padanna and Jahman opposite Tarn Taran; Dial and Bhasin opposite Amritsar; and Masrur Bara Bhai opposite the Bamiyal sector of Gurdaspur district, sources said.Possible cross-border collusionSources said security agencies were exploring ways to use online expressions of resentment by residents of Pakistani border villages, along with their own intelligence inputs, to build a case highlighting Pakistan’s alleged role in cross-border smuggling before the international community.The presence of Pakistan Rangers posts in the vicinity has raised questions among Indian security agencies about whether such operations could continue without the border force’s knowledge. Sources alleged possible collusion between smugglers and elements across the border, though any official complicity would require independent evidence.Some residents of Pakistani border villages have reportedly expressed resentment online over the alleged use of their localities by outsiders for smuggling, purportedly with the assistance of Pakistan Rangers. Security sources believe these videos and other public expressions of discontent could provide material for India to raise the issue through diplomatic channels and international forums.Anti-drone measures under scrutinyThe effectiveness of anti-drone systems deployed by the Centre and the Punjab government has also come under scrutiny, as repeated recoveries suggest that existing measures have not eliminated the threat.Possible collusion among smugglers, local facilitators and other elements cannot be ruled out, sources said.The alleged recovery of a weapon sourced from Amritsar, the use of encrypted communications and the suspected drone-smuggling networks have heightened security concerns.
